Model Earl’s plots as vertices in a graph, with an edge between two plots when the plots share a side (the usual grid adjacency).  Reading the spreadsheet’s color data produces ten green cells.  When those ten cells are linked by side-adjacency they break into three disconnected components:
1. (0,1),(1,1),(1,0),(2,1)
2. (0,4)
3. (2,4),(3,4),(3,3),(3,2),(4,4)
Because no edge joins one component to another, a path that stays entirely on green cells can never pass from one component to the next.  Therefore any walk starting on a green cell is confined to its own component and cannot visit every green cell.  Since Earl must traverse every plot he owns and return to the start without revisiting a plot, such a Hamiltonian cycle is impossible.

Black can exploit the alignment of the white king on g1 with the empty squares e1-f1 and the unprotected white queen on h5. Moving the queen from b3 to d1 gives check along the first rank.  
• If White interposes (2.Re1 or 2.Bf1) or sidesteps with 2.Kh2, the queen on h5 is captured next (2…Qxh5), leaving Black a full queen up.  
• If White captures the checking queen with 2.Qxd1, Black replies 2…Rxd1+, and after 3.Kh2 (or another forced move) 3…Rxd3 wins a bishop as well, giving Black a decisive material advantage.  
Thus 1…Qd1+ is the winning move.

The key is to start with a forcing check that either wins White’s queen outright or forces a queen exchange leaving Black with a clearly winning material advantage.

1…Qd1+ exploits the alignment of the Black queen on b3 and the White king on g1 along the first rank.

• If 2.Re1 / 2.Bf1 / 2.Be1, then 2…Qxh5 wins White’s queen immediately.
• If 2.Qxd1, then 2…Rxd1+ 3.Kh2 (or 3.Bf1) leaves Black up two pawns in a rook-and-minor-piece ending with the more active pieces and an exposed White king, an easily winning position.

No other White reply avoids decisive material loss, so 1…Qd1+ guarantees victory.

Because the only information given is the (purple-labelled) side-lengths, the green figure must be an axis-aligned (rectilinear) polygon whose successive sides measure 10, 6, 4, 8, 1, 1.5, 6, 4 and 1.  Tracing those lengths clockwise while alternating horizontal and vertical directions closes the path after a final 11.5-unit rise, producing the ten vertices
(0,0)→(10,0)→(10,−6)→(6,−6)→(6,−14)→(7,−14)→(7,−15.5)→(1,−15.5)→(1,−11.5)→(0,−11.5)→(0,0).
Applying the shoelace formula to those coordinates gives
|Σxᵢy_{i+1} − Σx_{i+1}yᵢ| ⁄ 2 = 229⁄2.
Hence the area of the polygon is 229⁄2 = 114.5 square units.
